title: The Prosecutor v. Ahmad Al Faqi Al Mahdi (attacks on historic and religious buildings in Timbuktu, Mali) - PARTIAL DRAFT
case_reference: ICC-01/12-01/15 (as cited in Wikipedia's reference list for the Reparations Order; not verified on an ICC page)
summary: PARTIAL: the ICC's own case pages and judgments could not be read (icc-cpi.int returned a bot-protection block page), so this entry rests on the Rome Statute text and on a Tier 4 Wikipedia article. As reported by Wikipedia, the ICC opened an investigation into the situation in Mali on 16 January 2013 after a referral by Mali, issued an arrest warrant for Ahmad Al Faqi Al Mahdi on 18 September 2015 alleging that between about 30 June and 10 July 2012 in Timbuktu he committed the war crime of intentionally directing attacks against historical monuments and buildings dedicated to religion, and he was surrendered to the Court on 26 September 2015. Wikipedia reports that he pleaded guilty at the start of his trial on 22 August 2016 to the destruction of nine mausoleums and a mosque, and that he was sentenced on 27 September 2016. Separately, UNESCO's World Heritage Committee, in Decision 40 COM 7A.6 (2016), congratulated Mali on rebuilding the 14 Saint mausoleums destroyed during the 2012 occupation of Timbuktu; that decision does not mention the ICC case.
legal_basis: The Rome Statute of the International Criminal Court (1998), as reproduced on the ICRC IHL Databases, lists among the war crimes in Article 8(2)(e)(iv), for armed conflicts not of an international character: 'Intentionally directing attacks against buildings dedicated to religion, education, art, science or charitable purposes, historic monuments, hospitals and places where the sick and wounded are collected, provided they are not military objectives'. Article 8(2)(b)(ix) contains the same wording for international armed conflicts. Wikipedia describes the charge in Al Mahdi in language that matches this provision, but the article number the Court itself applied was NOT read in an ICC document, so it is not asserted here.
outcome: PARTIAL, secondary source only. As reported by Wikipedia (citing ICC pages that could not be opened): Al Mahdi was sentenced on 27 September 2016 to nine years in prison after pleading guilty; a Reparations Order dated 17 August 2017 (cited as ICC-01/12-01/15) ordered individual, collective and symbolic reparations for the community of Timbuktu, and his liability was reportedly set at 2.7 million euros; on 25 November 2021 his sentence was reduced to seven years and he was released on 18 September 2022. Wikipedia describes the 2021 reduction both as 'commuted' and as 'reduced on appeal'; the procedure by which it happened was not verified and no appeal step is asserted here. The content of the judgment, the amounts of reparations beyond the single reported figure, and any implementation steps were not verified.
end_date_display: 2022-09-18 (release, as reported by Wikipedia; implementation of reparations not verified)

timeline.title: Alleged attacks on buildings in Timbuktu
timeline.description: As reported by Wikipedia, the arrest warrant alleges that between about 30 June and 10 July 2012 Al Mahdi committed the war crime of intentionally directing attacks against historical monuments and buildings dedicated to religion in Timbuktu; ten buildings are listed (nine mausoleums and the Sidi Yahya mosque).

timeline.title: ICC opens investigation in Mali
timeline.description: As reported by Wikipedia, the ICC opened a formal investigation after a referral of the situation by Mali, into alleged crimes since January 2012 in the context of an armed conflict in northern Mali.

timeline.title: Arrest warrant issued
timeline.description: As reported by Wikipedia, the ICC issued an arrest warrant for Al Mahdi on this date.

timeline.title: Surrender to the Court
timeline.description: As reported by Wikipedia, Niger surrendered Al Mahdi to the ICC and he was transferred to the Court's detention centre in The Hague.

timeline.title: Trial opens; guilty plea
timeline.description: As reported by Wikipedia, the trial began on 22 August 2016 and Al Mahdi pleaded guilty to destroying nine mausoleums and a mosque.

timeline.title: Judgment and sentence
timeline.description: As reported by Wikipedia, Al Mahdi was sentenced to nine years in prison. The judgment text itself was not read.

timeline.title: Reparations Order
timeline.description: As reported by Wikipedia, the ICC ordered individual, collective and symbolic reparations for the community of Timbuktu and set his liability at 2.7 million euros. The order itself was not read.

timeline.title: Sentence reduced to seven years
timeline.description: As reported by Wikipedia, his sentence was reduced to seven years (Wikipedia uses both 'commuted' and 'reduced on appeal'; the procedure was not verified).

timeline.title: Release
timeline.description: As reported by Wikipedia, Al Mahdi was released on this date.

sources.title: Timbuktu
sources.reliability_note: Site profile: inscribed 1988 under criteria (ii), (iv), (v); three great mosques (Djingareyber, Sankore, Sidi Yahia) and sixteen mausoleums; on the List in Danger since 2012. Does not discuss the ICC case.

sources.title: Decision 40 COM 7A.6: Timbuktu (Mali) (C 119rev)
sources.reliability_note: 40th session, Istanbul, 2016. Congratulates Mali on reconstruction of the 14 Saint mausoleums destroyed during the 2012 occupation and retains Timbuktu on the List in Danger. Does not mention the ICC or Al Mahdi; the number 14 is UNESCO's and must not be blended with the ICC's nine mausoleums and a mosque.
